Tischfield* *Department of Medical and Molecular Genetics, Indiana University School of Medicine, Indianapolis; tDepartment of Pediatrics, Saint Joseph's Hospital, Reykjavik; *Department of Pediatrics, Royal Free Hospital, London; and §Department of Anatomy and Cell Biology, University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, Cincinnati Summary We have completely sequenced the adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) gene from each of six patients - five (IV) from Iceland and one (VI) from Britain. Cases I and II shared a common ancestor six and seven generations ago, and cases I and V shared a common ancestor seven generations ago, but cases III and IV were unrelated to the above or to each other, over seven generations.

Genomic DNA was amplified by PCR, subcloned into M13mpl8, and sequenced. Genomic and PCRamplified DNAs were also analyzed by restrictionenzyme digestion and Southern blotting. The same missense mutation was identified in all six patients.

This mutation leads to the replacement of asp (GAC) by val (GTC), at amino acid position 65. The gene sequences from all patients were otherwise identical to our wildtype sequence. The homozygous nature of the mutation was confirmed by sequencing the PCR product directly.

All six patients were homozygous for the 1.25kb TaqI RFLP. The Icelandic patients were also homozygous for the 8kb SphI RFLP, but the British patient was heterozygous at this site. These studies suggest that a founder effect is likely to be responsible for APRT deficiency in the Icelandic population.

The finding of the same mutation in a patient from Britain suggests that this mutation may have originated in mainland Europe. Introduction Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT; E.C. 2.4.2.7) is a purinemetabolism enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of AMP from adenine and 5phos- phoribosyll-pyrophosphate. In patients with complete APRT deficiency (McKusick 102600), adenine is oxidized, by xanthine oxidase, to the highly insoluble and nephrotoxic derivative, 2,8dihydroxyadenine (DHA).

This produces crystalluria and can lead to kidneystone formation and eventual renal failure (Simmonds et al. 1989). 1306 Two phenotypic variants of APRT deficiency have been recognized, but the pattern of clinical expression in the two types is similar. Type II deficiency (complete enzyme deficiency in vivo but partial deficiency in cell extracts) has been found only in Japan.

Type II patients are homozygotes or compound heterozygotes for the APR T*J missense mutation in exon 5 (Kamatani et al. 1987, 1990b; Hidaka et al. 1988; Sahota et al. 1990). Type I APRT deficiency (complete deficiency in vivo or in vitro), on the other hand, has been found in patients from many different countries. Type I patients are homozygotes or compound heterozygotes for a variety of null alleles collectively designated APRT*QO (Fujimori et al. 1985;
Hidaka et al. 1987). To date, three different QO mutant alleles have been identified (Hidaka et al. 1987; Sahota et al. 1990).

In the present report we describe the identification of a single missense mutation (GAC"GTC) in exon 3 (aspOsval) in all five patients with type I APRT APRT Deficiency in Iceland 1307 deficiency reported from Iceland and in a patient from Britain. Patients and Methods Patients Icelandic cases IIV have been described elsewhere (Laxdal and Jonasson 1988). Case V is a 42year-old Icelandic woman whom we have identified recently.

Her clinical history is similar to those of most of the previously described adult cases (Simmonds et al. 1989). She had recurrent urinarytract infections from age 10 years. Her first renal colic occurred at age 23 years, and she has had recurrent attacks since then.

Bilateral nephrolithotomy was performed at age 29 years. She passed a right ureteral stone in December 1989, and at that time typical DHA crystals were noticed by microscopy of the urine. The composition of the stone was confirmed by UV and infrared spectroscopy.

She was started on allopurinol in March 1990, and, at a dose of 200 mg/d, the urine crystals disappeared. Cases I (AJ) and II (HH) shared common ancestors six and seven generations ago, and cases I and V (HS) had common ancestors seven generations ago (fig. 1). Cases III (PJ) and IV (HE) are not known to be interrelated or to show any relationship to the other three cases, over at least seven generations.

The maternal grandfather of case II is of British descent (fig. 1). Case VI (SB), now age 14 years, is a patient from Britain and has been described elsewhere (Greenwood et al. 1982). In brief, she presented at age 4 years with renal failure due to DHA lithiasis.

She was comatose, anuric, and required peritoneal dialysis. Ultrasonography and retrograde pyelography showed the presence of bilateral renal caliculi. The stones were removed by pyelolithotomy and were identified as DHA.

This case is not known to have any relationship to the Icelandic cases. Methods Blood collected in sodium heparincontaining vacutainers was sent by air to Indianapolis from Iceland and Britain. The amplification conditions were as follows: 0.5 Ig DNA, 0.4 jg each primer (see below), 1.2 mM MgC12, 0.2 mM each deoxyribonucleotide, 5% dimethylsulfoxide, 1 min denaturation at 951C, 1 min annealing at 600C, 4 min extension at 720C, and 30 cycles. The initial denaturation of the template was for 7 min in a boilingwater bath.

Other conditions were as described in the GeneAmp manual. Primers NC720 (sense sequence) and C719 (antisense sequence), located at positions - 161 to - 140 and 2242 to 2221, respectively, of our wildtype sequence, were used for amplification (Chen et al. 1991). (The of the ATG start codon is designated base 1.)

The primer sequences (5' to 3') were ATGGCGCCTAGGAGTCCATGAA (NC720) and TGGGATCCAGCTGGAGATGTTG (C719). The PCR reaction mixture was electrophoresed on an agarose gel, and the 2.4kb fragment was purified from the gel by using GeneClean (BIO 101; La Jolla, CA). Approximately 200 ng PCRamplified DNA was then ligated with 50 ng M13mpl8 RF DNA which had been digested with HincII.

After Escherichia coli JM109 transformation, singlestranded DNA from three to five positive plaques from each patient was sequenced completely (Chen et al. 1991). The PCRamplified DNA from each patient was also sequenced directly. For RFLP analysis, genomic DNA was digested with SphI and PCRamplified DNA was digested with TaqI.

The SphI digests were electrophoresed on agarose gels, were transferred to GeneScreen Plus membranes, and were probed with the 2.2kb BamHI fragment of the APRT gene (Stambrook et al. 1984). Prehybridization and hybridization conditions were as 1308 Chen et al. described in the GeneScreen instruction manual. The TaqI digests were electrophoresed on agarose gels and stained with ethidium bromide.

The polymorphic Sphl site lies outside the APRT gene and is 2.8 kb upstream (Kamatani et al. 1 990a) of the polymorphic TaqI site, which is located within intron 2 (Chen et al. 1991). Nucleic acid and protein sequences were analyzed using the Microgenie (V5.0) software from Beckman. All patients were deficient in enzyme activity; the low level of activity seen in cases II, III, and V is not significantly different from the background. Lymphoblast extracts from the patients showed <1% activity of the control mean (614 nmol/h/mg, SD = 26, n = 6). An Ato-T transversion at position 1350 (exon 3) was identified in all five Icelandic patients (fig. 2).

The homozygous nature of the mutation in all six patients was confirmed by direct sequencing of PCRamplified DNA. This mutation predicts the replacement of asp (GAC) by val (GTC) at amino acid position 65. All six patients were homozygous for the 1.25kb TaqI RFLP, as observed in digests of PCRamplified DNA.

The digest pattern for three of these patients (Icelandic cases IIII) and for two control subjects is shown in figure 3. The 1.25kb fragment seen in TaqI digests of PCRamplified DNA is equivalent to the 2.1kb fragment seen in digests of genomic DNA (Stambrook et al. 1984; Chen et al. 1991).

All five Icelandic patients were homozygous for the 8kb SphI RFLP. The three sons of case III, the mother of case IV, and the British patient (case VI) were heterozygous at this site (fig. 4). Discussion An exon 3 missense mutation (GACGTC at position 1350, asp65sval) was identified in all five Icelandic patients (IV) who had APRT deficiency.

Patients I and II are related six and seven generations back, and patients I and IV are related seven generations back, (fig. 1), but patients III and IV are not demonstrably related either to any of these three or to each other, over seven generations. It seems most likely, however, that the mutation in all five patients has a common ancestral origin, since most Icelanders are discovered to be interrelated if the genealogy is followed back 1214 generations. The 0.5kb fragment in all five lanes results from an invariant TaqI site in exon 2 (Chen et al. 1991). The 1.91kb fragment (1.25 + 0.66 kb) in lanes 4 and 5 is due to the loss of the polymorphic TaqI site in intron 2 and is equivalent to the 2.8kb fragment seen in genomic digests (Stambrook et al. 1984). Flanking regions from these patients supports the notion of common ancestry.

It also suggests that the mutation may be of relatively recent origin. The same missense mutation was found in the British patient (VI) but not in four other European patients we have examined (data not shown). Since the maternal grandfather ofpatient II is of British origin (fig. 1), one of the mutant alleles from this patient could have come from Britain, but it is equally likely that the 1309 mutant allele came from the paternal grandfather, who is Icelandic.

It is also possible that the mutation in the Icelandic patients and in the British patient are of independent origin. Sufficient family data are not available to differentiate between these possibilities. It is unlikely that the GAC triplet encoding asp65 is a hot spot for mutation, since we have not seen this particular mutation in 13 other type I patients from different groups (data not shown).

SphI digestion of genomic DNA from all five Icelandic cases gave a 8kb fragment on a Southern blot. Digestion of DNA from the three sons of case III, from the mother of case IV, and from case VI gave 8- and 12kb fragments, indicating the presence of both APR T alleles (fig. 4). The Icelandic patients are most likely to be homozygotes at this site, but the possibility of a deletion of one of the APR T alleles cannot be ruled out.

Previous studies have shown that the APR T*t mutation in patients with type II deficiency has a common ancestral origin (Kamatani et al. 1987, 1990a; Hidaka et al. 1988). We and others have recently identified a common nonsense mutation in exon 3 in Japanese patients with type I APRT deficiency (Sahota et al. 1990; Mimori et al. 1991). We have also shown that the previously described mutation at the intron 4 splicedonor site in one allele from a Belgian family is a common cause of APRT deficiency in the Caucasian population (Hidaka et al. 1987; Gathof et al., in press).

The finding of another common mutation, APRTIC, .id, suggests that a few different mutations is likely to be responsible for the majority of reported cases of APRT deficiency. The APRTIceland mutation occurs in a 11amino- acid stretch that is fully conserved among human, mouse, and hamster APRTs. This region also shows extensive homology with the enzyme from Drosophila melanogaster. The sequence of the Escherichia coli enzyme in this region differs from the above sequence at several positions, but the differences are all neutral substitutions (Johnson et al. 1987)

(fig. 5). The GAC--GTC mutation, resulting in an asp6s--val substitution, is the only change, visa'-vis the wildtype sequence, that we have identified in the six patients described here. The asp6s--val substitution in the enzyme predicts both a change from hydrophilicity to hydrophobicity and a change in secondary structure from 3sheet/random coil/ Pturn to 1sheet.

The loss of enzyme activity after this substitution suggests that asp6s is important for structural or functional integrity of the enzyme.
